#1907. Breaking: The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4073 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.
  • “The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr.
  • Industry observers note that monteon and Cole continue scuffling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.

“The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”.

Industry observers note that monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.

The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.

“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.

“And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”.

Sources indicate that I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.

Filmmaker Vince Nett captures the shirtless shenanigans of Carlos Monteon Jr.

Recent findings suggest that cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that says “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.

The house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: Newly introduced Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.

These guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.

Part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is currently facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.

Left to right: Jonathan Jacobs, Chris Petrone, and Johnny Cole collaborate on a social media house-tour video.

It has been revealed that during the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he states, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”.

Industry observers note that of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.

It has been revealed that “I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”.

Sources indicate that this is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole notes.

According to recent reports, of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole says.

An activity at the Hey Brother House where members offer gifts to the group and request actions they would like to receive from others.

In selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.

I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.).

I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.

Later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon states afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”.

Cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he says, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.).

It has been revealed that the next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.

Journaling is a popular practice at the Hey Brother House.

Sources indicate that “It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.

Industry observers note that if they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy indicates.

In a recent development, the Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.

Instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones said. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”.

Industry observers note that even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—rapidly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he states. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”.

Sources indicate that the bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole claims embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then indicates a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.

Recent findings suggest that then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.

“Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright notes. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”.

Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.

The group holds a meeting to talk through a conflict that has caused tension. Facing camera, left to right: Chris Petrone and Johnny Cole. Facing away, from left to right: Ian Lightfoot and Jerry Zeng.

In a recent development, “I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been remarked offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he states. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”.

The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”.

The vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”.

“In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's important to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.

On the third floor, the day after the tense emotional group meeting, all that remains is a box of tissues.

Recent findings suggest that immediately, someone notes that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”.

Echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he indicates.

Sources indicate that the tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright says he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”.

Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation said that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.

Sources indicate that he isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).

Josh Kennedy (left) and Johnny Cole have a heartfelt conversation while doing the dishes.

Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he claims. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”.

All told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.

According to recent reports, little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, claims some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.

Josh Kennedy (left) cheers on Johnny Cole and Ian Lightfoot as they hug after their dance-off performances at The Movement Project.

But there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.

There was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel reveals Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.

I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he stated. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

It has been revealed that but what about other e-readers? The best deal outside of Kindles is on the Kobo Libra Colour, which is down to $229.99. That saves you $30 off its MSRP of $259.99. On Oct. 1, Amazon dropped a redesigned collection of Kindles. We've tested the latest e-readers and named the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition the best overall e-reader.

As of September 2026, we've added the Boox Go 6 to this guide, naming it the best Kindle alternative. We also named the Kindle Paperwhite the best e-reader for the beach (in addition to being the best overall) and named the Durobo Krono the best e-reader for audiobooks.

In August 2026, Amazon increased the price of Kindles. Now the basic Kindle costs $149.99 ($40 increase) and the Kindle Paperwhite costs $199.99 ($40 increase).

Industry observers note that in July 2026, Boox announced it was releasing a pocket-sized e-reader, the Picco. After IFA 2026, rumors floated that the Boox Picco would be released in November 2026.

Read our full review of the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026).

Sources indicate that pretty much everyone: If Amazon is pretty intrinsic to your spending, then going for a Kindle, specifically the Paperwhite Signature Edition, makes the most sense. While we previously saw it as an upgrade pick, the upcoming aluminum casing makes it essential with a sleeker, sturdier case. It turns pages without stuttering, never slowing down when you’re in the thick of the action.

Beach readers: It's also the best e-reader for the beach. The screen is vibrant and has adjustable brightness, meaning it can adapt when transitioning from reading in bright sunlight to dimmer indoors. You can adjust the brightness manually or set it to automatically adjust. It also comes with adjustable screen warmth, perfect for evening readers who want to give their eyes a chance to relax. It’s lightweight and fits comfortably in small crossbody bags. Plus, it’s waterproof, keeping it safe from poolside vacations and spilled water bottles in bags.

The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition dethrones the 2024 Kindle Paperwhite as the best overall e-reader. Historically, I've preferred the Paperwhite, finding that the Signature Edition doesn't have enough features to justify its price, but the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition finally fixes that. With a newly introduced aluminum case, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition feels like a high-end piece of tech. With a thinner body and square edges, this new Kindle feels more like a smartphone or tablet than it does an e-reader.

But inside the more advanced chassis is still the same e-reader you love. It's fast with a high-contrast 300 ppi resolution. The matte display is glare-free and easy on the eyes. With adjustable warmth and brightness, you can read with it in bright summer sun at the beach and then turn it down and warm it up when you're in a dim bedroom. And speaking of the beach, its IPX8 rating makes it safe to use in the bath or at the pool.

It is a more expensive e-reader at $249.99, especially compared to the Paperwhite's $199.99, but here's what you get for an extra $50. The upgraded aluminum case makes that $50 nearly worth it compared to the plastic exterior of the Paperwhite, but the Signature Edition also has an ad-free lockscreen, 32GB of storage compared to the Paperwhite's 16GB, wireless charging, auto-adjusting brightness, and best of all, compatibility with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover.

Industry observers note that plus, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition comes in more exciting color options. While the Paperwhite just comes in graphite, the Signature Edition also comes in a stunning seaglass green.

Recent findings suggest that don't get us wrong, though; we still love the Kindle Paperwhite. If you want to save $50, the next best e-reader you can buy is the basic Kindle Paperwhite. It's still a quick, well-rounded e-reader but doesn't come in fun colors and has lockscreen ads.

Read our full review of the Kobo Clara Colour.

Recent findings suggest that for those who want an Amazon alternative: If you're just diving into the world of e-readers and not particularly thrilled about Kindles and their Amazon ties, then the Kobo Clara is the right answer. It offers a color display for those who enjoy manga and graphic novels, but it remains speedy with fast processing when turning pages or swapping between books.

Recent findings suggest that libby users: It's especially great for Libby users, who want seamless integration with books that automatically load into your library as soon as you borrow them. While Kindle's Libby integration only works in the U.S., the Kobo works with Libby no matter where you live.

Industry observers note that having tried my hand at more than a dozen e-readers in all shapes, sizes, and brands, I wasn't expecting to be so deeply impressed by the Kobo Clara Colour, but it is a wonderful e-reader. With a 6-inch screen, it's slightly smaller than the Kindle Paperwhite, but it allows you to hold it comfortably for multiple hours at a time without any wrist or arm fatigue.

It has been revealed that in my previous testing with Kobo devices, I've really liked them, but one sticking point is that they're slower than Kindles. Initially, I found that the Kobo Clara kept up with the Paperwhite, but after several months of use, it had a tendency to lag. Compared to Kindles, I had to manually sync the Kobo Clara to get my library books to show up.

Its processing system is otherwise really smart and fixes one of my biggest e-reader pet peeves. When you adjust the font size on a Kindle, the device doesn't recalculate how many pages are in the book, making it inaccurate, so you don't know exactly how many pages you have left in a chapter. The Kobo Clara does recalculate page count accurately for a more exact reading experience. Though, one thing to note: Kobo counts the number of digital pages, whereas Kindle page numbers typically match up with physical book copies.

For the same price as the Kindle Paperwhite, the Kobo Clara offers color displays, something you can't get in the Kindle lineup unless you're willing to spend $250. The colors aren't as bright as you'd experience in a physical book, but they're still vivid enough to enjoy a graphic novel.

The Kobo Clara's biggest downfall is its battery life. It's supposed to last up to 42 days, although many online people say it averages out at about two weeks. That's quite pathetic in the face of the Kindle's 12-week battery life; however, I'd trade in a better reading experience over a couple weeks of battery life any day.

Read our full review of the Durobo Krono.

Across app readers: If your digital library is sprawling — you have books through Kindle, Kobo, Libby, and Audible — then you need an e-reader that can access all of them. Durobo's Krono e-reader is a compact e-reader that basically functions like a tablet. Most e-readers on this list are Androids, but none have open Android systems that let you download the apps you want, as the Krono does.

Audiobook lovers: For the audiobook lovers, the Durobo Krono also plays audio in addition to transcribing it. With access to the Google Play store available, you can download any app you read on to access your digital library, including Audible, Libro.fm, and Spotify. However, if you have a collection of EPUB files, you can also download them directly to Krono's library.

Having tried several other open Android e-readers, I haven't been impressed. The Remarkable Paper Pro is way too substantial and the Boox Go is too slow and too difficult to get books on, so I wasn't expecting much from the Durobo Krono. Turns out, it is a phenomenal e-reader.

Recent findings suggest that since I test e-readers for a living, my digital library is spread out across all different platforms. Rather than balancing a bunch of different e-readers, the Krono puts both my Kindle and Kobo libraries on one device. The only library I don't have access to is Apple Books, since it's unavailable in the Google Play Store.

It has been revealed that the Durobo Krono is the perfect size, with a 6.13-inch display, similar to the basic Kindle. It has a matte display with 300 ppi resolution. It also has a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth.

Powered by an octa-core processor, it moves quickly between apps and books. It easily competed with the speed of both Kindles and Kobos; however, it can get bogged down. It runs the Kindle app, Libby, and Libro.fm no problem. But some apps, like Substack, slowed it down with their high internet demands. Once I deleted the Substack app, though, it got back to normal.

As someone who loves to read while listening to the audiobook, I also love that I can do both on one device. I can listen to an audiobook on Audible while reading the EPUB file alongside it. The Krono also has voice transcription and note-taking capabilities, a nice bonus feature, but not essential in an e-reader.

Read our full review of the Boox Go 6 (Gen II).

You want an e-reader that does more: If you want to do more on an e-reader, like check your Storygraph or browse Libby, then you'll need one with an open system. The Boox Go 6 (Gen II) runs on an Android 11 system with access to the Google Play Store, so you can download any app to your e-reader. Yes, it could lead to more distractions, but with an E Ink display, it still feels more analog than a classic iPad or Android tablet.

But you want it to look like an e-reader: The Boox Go 6 (Gen II) doesn't look like a tablet, though. The E Ink display provides a matte, black and white background with 300 ppi resolution, so it's gentle on the eyes. It's the same size as a basic Kindle but with the flush front design of a Paperwhite, so it gives you the best of both worlds.

The Boox Go 6 (Gen II) is the brand's answer to Amazon's Kindle. With a 6-inch screen, it fits comfortably in your hand for hours of reading. With an open Android system, you can download any app in the Google Play Store, so you can access any book across any app, including Kindle, Rakuten Kobo, and Libby.

Recent findings suggest that it's the perfect size and shape to hold for hours at a time. Boox even sells a MagSafe case so you can pop on a PopSockets grip for an ergonomic hold. Boox e-readers do have a bit of a learning curve, as the E Ink display requires a bit of tinkering. But once you get it set up, it's extremely customizable.

According to recent reports, because it can tackle a lot of apps rather than just doing one thing like a Kindle, it needs some extra power behind it. Unfortunately, it doesn't quite have it. The Boox Go 6 suffers from significant lag and screen response challenges that make it occasionally frustrating to use. It's slower than either a Kindle or a Kobo, but it's a consolation you'll have to make if you want an e-reader that does more.

Industry observers note that miniature enthusiasts: If you want an e-reader that you can have on you at all times and even slip in your pocket, there are so few options out there. That's what makes the Xetink X4 so special. It's a truly tiny e-reader with a 4.3-inch display; but with a built-in magnet, it can attach to MagSafe devices so you can keep it attached to your iPhone.

In a recent development, you must love DRM ePUBs: If you think you're getting a mini Kindle, you're not. Instead, expect a tiny e-reader that is a great fit for turning online articles into PDFs or collecting all the free ePUBs. It's not compatible with any DRM files.

Recent findings suggest that in such a little package, the Xetink X4 feels like it should be a toy, but it's actually a solid e-reader. It's the smallest e-reader we've tested, measuring 4.3 inches, so you can slip it in your pocket and go. That small display, while convenient on the go, won't be suitable for all eyes, especially if you like to crank up the text size on your e-reader or phone.

In a recent development, the resolution of the Xetink X4 is 219 ppi, which is lower res than you'll find on most e-readers. It also includes page-turning buttons along the bottom of the e-reader. Xteink has a great transfer system, too. It's similar to Amazon's Send to Kindle feature, in that you can send EPUBs and articles to the e-reader. The ability to send articles is particularly compelling, so you can send your reading list to your e-reader and enjoy them in one spot.

Sources indicate that my biggest matter with the Xetink X4 is how few files it supports, as you can't access Libby books or any DRM files on it. If you are going to commit, you'll have to be OK with reading primarily free EPUB files. However, folks at Lifehacker figured out how to install different firmware onto the device for a better reading experience.

Read our full review of the Kindle (2026).

In a recent development, quality on a budget: If you want to dip your toes into e-readers, the standard Kindle model is the best budget-friendly model. Like the Paperwhite, it has 16GB of storage, with room for thousands of books. It’s the smallest Kindle, and you won’t miss the size of the Paperwhite. Instead, you’ll be delighted that it’s genuinely pocket-sized. Plus, if you want an e-reader with some flair, it’s now available in black and ube. Plus, the 2026 version even has two aluminum options in alpine sky or seaglass green.

In a recent development, amazon made some updates to the 2026 Kindle that make it worthy of its higher price tag. It has a fresh, flush front design for a sleeker look. Plus, the design team made a change we've been dying for — they moved the power button to the side of the device. Plenty of specs have stayed the same between generations. It still has a 6-inch screen, 300 ppi resolution, and six weeks of battery life.

According to recent reports, what truly makes it stand out is just how lightweight it is. The 2026 Kindle weighs 18 grams (.66 ounces) less than the previous generation and it's a noticeable difference. It feels like you're barely holding anything; plus, it's even better for travel as it takes up very little space and weighs just half a pound.

It has been revealed that it's a speedy little e-reader, too. Its screen is responsive and loads books within seconds. The only thing that could make the e-reader better is if Amazon added an adjustable warm light and made it waterproof. However, according to Amazon, the lack of those features keeps it affordable.

The device is now available in its basic format in either ube or graphite. However, it's also available with an aluminum backing, making it more like a tablet. The aluminum Kindle is more expensive at $189.99, but it does come with 32GB of storage and two additional color options.

Read our full review of the Kobo Libra Colour.

Color enthusiasts and graphic novel readers: For serious readers who don't mind splurging a little, the Kobo Libra Colour delivers an upgraded e-reader experience. With a similar seven-inch display, the Libra Colour offers two features the Kindle Paperwhite cannot: Color and note-taking. Book covers, in-book illustrations, and photos are all featured in color with the Libra.

Industry observers note that annotators and highlighters: And if you're an annotator, you can highlight and mark up your pages in different colors to stay organized. In the Kindle family, only the Scribe supports scribbling, and with a higher price tag.

Recent findings suggest that bathtub readers: It's equipped with more than enough storage at 32GB and is waterproof. Plus, if you were devastated by the discontinuation of the Kindle Oasis, the Libra Colour offers a similar design that includes page-turning buttons.

If you were to ask me which e-reader to buy, it's a real toss-up between the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition and the Kobo Libra Colour. While the Kobo Libra Colour is expensive at $259.99, it's worth its price tag for all its included features.

Above all, the Kobo Libra Colour has the best ergonomic design. It's more square than a Kindle, as one side offers extra space for page-turning buttons. This makes it easier to hold, especially while lying down and reading one-handed. It's one of the few e-readers to have an internal gyroscope, so when you rotate the device, the display rotates with it. While reading in bed, if I flipped over, I could rotate the device to still be able to hold it on the side with page-turning buttons.

Recent findings suggest that while the color display on the Kobo is nice, it is still rather muted. While reading Heartstopper, the colors were quite toned down in comparison to how they appeared on the iPad Mini. The Libra Colour's battery life isn't as strong as a Kindle Paperwhite's. While testing the Kobo Libra Colour over 10 weeks, my colleague Bethany Allard had to charge the device twice. Plus, it's a bit slower than a Kindle, with the occasional stall while switching between books.

While the Kindle may have the Kobo beat on processing and battery life, I still think the Libra Colour is a worthy upgrade as it offers the best design of an e-reader with the perk of color. Amazon's color e-reader, the Colorsoft, costs $289.99, so at $259.99, the Libra is a little cheaper.

Young readers: If you're raising a voracious reader, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is the best e-reader for kids. It's waterproof, which means it stands up to juice spills and dips in the pool. Plus, it comes with a built-in case. It's designed to be kid-proof, not just physically, but also with built-in parental controls. If you're concerned about monitoring your kid's bookshelf, this Kindle allows you to approve downloads by kids and displays age-friendly titles that kids can easily access.

Industry observers note that one area where Amazon has all other e-reader brands beat is in the kids market. There are special kid-friendly models of the basic Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. Our preferred model for kids is the Kindle Paperwhite Kids.

More than anything else, an e-reader for kids has to be waterproof, which is why the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is the best choice. It comes with everything we like about the standard Paperwhite: a beautiful, high-resolution screen that works faster than any previous generation.

But what makes it great for kids is that it's a distraction-free device. It doesn't come with ads, notifications, or the temptation of games or video. I also like that it's a bit heavier than the standard Paperwhite, giving it a sturdier design. Plus, the built-in case adds an extra level of protection.

It has been revealed that the parental controls are easy to use and set up, and the device also comes with a six-month free subscription to Amazon Kids+, which provides unlimited access to thousands of age-appropriate books. The library of books is easy for kids to navigate and offers classics like Lois Lowry's The Giver and modern classics like Diary of a Wimpy Kid.

It has been revealed that what I don't love is the price. At $229.99, it's more expensive than the standard Paperwhite. If you want to go for a budget kids' pick, I'd recommend the standard Kindle, which you can set up as a kids' device during setup to ensure parental controls and add an Amazon Kids+ subscription for $5.99 per month. Plus, as your kid ages, you won't have to upgrade to a more teen-friendly e-reader.

Read our full review of the Kindle Scribe (3rd Generation).

Recent findings suggest that for annotators and journalers: If, looking through your bookshelf, your books have dog-eared pages, highlighted lines, and scribbles in the margins, your instinct might be that an e-reader isn't for you, but I'd like to introduce you to the Kindle Scribe. It's the only Kindle with writing capabilities and comes with an included stylus pen that magnetically attaches to the side of the e-reader; it's ready for all your handwritten thoughts.

The pen moves nicely across the screen, mimicking the texture of writing on paper. In addition to a library of books, the Kindle Scribe also comes with a journal section where you can take notes. The notes feature is especially great for students who want to handwrite notes and convert their handwriting into text.

It has been revealed that the 2025 Kindle Scribe got a much-needed upgrade. All the good stuff has held over with the addition of some major improvements.

Sources indicate that it's still massive, with an 11-inch display, which does make it a little more awkward to hold while reading, but for writing or annotating, it's optimal. Unlike other tablets (I'm looking at you, iPads) that require you to buy a pen separately, the Kindle Scribe comes with a pen that conveniently attaches to the side so it doesn't get lost. However, it's not the most secure magnetic hold, so be careful not to bump the pen off accidentally.

Writing on the Kindle Scribe is a joy. Before testing this e-reader, I used my iPad and Apple Pencil to annotate readings, but I never loved it because the screen felt too slick for the Apple Pencil. The Kindle Scribe does not suffer this problem, as the matte screen lends some friction to the pen, making it feel like you're writing on paper. I enjoyed writing with the pen, and I swear my handwriting looked better on the Kindle Scribe than on my iPad.

In a recent development, it finally got a processing update that makes it as speedy as every other Kindle. Gone is the lag when switching between journals and books. Plus, the displays have greatly improved, too, as the 2025 Kindle Scribe has virtually no ghosting. Like the Kindle Paperwhite, the Scribe's battery life lasts 12 weeks. It also has storage options, with 32GB and 64GB versions available.

It's not your only option if you want a Kindle that can write. The Scribe Colorsoft is also available, and while we appreciate that model, it's quite a bit more expensive. The 2025 Scribe is a better value; it just doesn't have the wow factor of color.

Read our full review of the Apple iPad mini.

It has been revealed that single device consumers: There are so many devices that the modern person is meant to have. If adding an e-reader seems superfluous, I'd recommend a tablet that allows you to read books, stream indicates, and browse the internet. The best tablet for reading? It's the iPad mini.

Recent findings suggest that but why is this iPad better than any other? It's all about the size. At 8.3 inches, it comfortably sits in your hand and is about the same size as a paperback.

Sources indicate that before testing these e-readers, I read using my 9th-generation iPad, and my main complaint was always the size. After 30 minutes of reading, my hand and wrist would strain holding up all 10.2 inches of the screen. That's why the 8.3-inch display of the iPad mini was such a treat. Reading with the mini made me feel like I was holding an actual book rather than a laptop screen.

Unsurprisingly, the iPad mini has the most computing power of all the e-readers on this list. It jumps between apps and turns pages without an ounce of hesitation. Plus, it offers the most expansive ways to read books. You can read using Apple's built-in Apple Books app or download and read within the Kindle and Libby apps. And unlike most e-readers, you can read comics and graphic novels in full color. Plus, it has far more storage than any other e-reader, as the 7th generation iPad mini starts at 128GB of storage.

According to recent reports, despite my love of the iPad mini, I have some beef, most of which is with the screen. While I love its overall size, it has a substantial glare problem. I've found this to be true with any iPad I've read on; the slick glass screen has a glare in almost any environment. That's no surprise in the sun, but even at night, I found the screen to be a little too shiny, causing my eyes to have some trouble focusing. This does have a fix; if you want your iPad screen to look more like the matte of a Kindle, a screen protector such as Paperlike creates that effect.

Sources indicate that additionally, compared to e-readers, which provide months of battery life, the iPad mini only gets you hours. If you're reading for a couple of hours a day, you're probably only charging the iPad once a week, which isn't a substantial deal but certainly more than a traditional e-reader.

Topics Amazon Books iPad Kindle E-Readers.

According to recent reports, when picking an e-reader, price is always a consideration. However, almost all e-readers fall into the same price range. Kindle and Kobo e-readers both start around $149.99/$159.99, while the tiny Boox Picco is just $109.99. If you want handwriting capabilities, Kobo and Boox make the most affordable options, as Kindle's Scribes start at $500.

Industry observers note that remarkable PaperPro: Whenever you search for e-readers, Remarkable's tablets will always pop up in the search results, but unfortunately, it's hard to obtain ePUB files on the Remarkable. With Remarkable, you can access files within Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive. If you have any locked ePUB files — like from Libby — you won't be able to access them on a Remarkable tablet. So, after testing the Remarkable tablet myself, it proved to be a better document reader or digital journal than an e-reader.

Onyx Boox Go 7: While we love the Boox Go 6, we didn't love the Go 7. It's the same size as the Kobo Libra or Amazon Kindle, but it really lags on processing speed. Reading ePUB files from Libby required downloading the Adobe Digital Editions app onto the Boox Go 7, and there was significant lag when opening and closing the app. While it was an easier process than getting library books on a Nook, it was still a major pain compared to Kindle or Kobo's integrations. The Boox Go 7 lagged and took ages to load files. I was most looking forward to testing this Boox because of its page-turning buttons, but unfortunately, I found that they didn't work on my device.

Boox Palma 2: I loved reading on the Boox Palma. It's a really solid palm-sized e-reader with an open Android system, so you can download any reading app from the Google Play store, including Libby, Kindle, and Kobo. Unfortunately, the Palma 2 is being discontinued, and its availability is dwindling, which is why it's not included in this list.

In terms of major-name e-readers, you might notice one omission from this list: the Barnes & Noble Nook. I have tested this e-reader, and it was previously featured on this list. However, after testing more devices, it no longer makes the cut. In comparison to any of the Kindles or the Kobo Libra, the Nook has sloth-like performance, making it frustrating to use.

Sources indicate that plus, getting my library books onto the Nook was a nightmare, as it was a multi-step process that required downloading to a computer before uploading to a Nook. Its only redeeming quality was the buttons on either side of the device, which made page turning a breeze. However, unless you are a loyal buyer of Barnes & Noble books, I recommend steering clear of the Nook.

Once you get an e-reader, it's time to fill it up with books, and that doesn't necessarily mean spending money. In fact, you can load up your e-reader without spending a dime; you just need to be a bit resourceful.

According to recent reports, the best way to read nearly any book — a classic or hot fresh release — is with Libby. I have read hundreds of free books with the Libby app — I wouldn't have been able to test for this guide without it. It connects with your library card, allowing you to borrow from your local library's digital collection. Plus, both Kobo and Kindle have exceptional Libby integrations.

It has been revealed that another way to build your library is through Stuff Your Kindle Day events. These are 24-hour opportunities led by authors that make books discounted or free.

If you're a fan of the classics or looking to discover a treasure lost to time, an online resource like Project Gutenberg has more than 75,000 books in the public domain that you can download and read on an e-reader.

It has been revealed that the best Kindle is the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, dethroning the standard Paperwhite. Overall, it strikes the right balance of performance and value, while possessing everything we want in an e-reader. The standard Kindle is great for those on a budget, but it's not waterproof, and while the basic Paperwhite is always a favorite, the Signature Edition aluminum case and extra features make it the best e-reader you can buy.

Our two favorite e-readers come from Kindle and Kobo, but is one better than the other? It depends on what you're looking for. If performance is your primary concern, then a Kindle, specifically the Paperwhite, is better as it outperforms the Kobo Libra Colour in terms of speed when turning pages or loading books. However the Kobo Clara Colour measures up to the Paperwhite's performance.

It has been revealed that if you're looking to de-Amazon your life, then a Kobo e-reader is the better e-reader. It offers all the things we like in a Kindle, such as Libby integration, adjustable brightness and warmth, a waterproof rating, and an overall better-designed package. While Amazon discontinued its Kindle Oasis, an e-reader with page-turning buttons, the Kobo Libra Colour has not abandoned this fan-favorite design. It also features an internal gyroscope so you can rotate the Kobo for a better ergonomic experience.

Yes, you can read on an iPad, and as an iPad reader, I highly recommend it. iPads come with the Apple Books app. However, other reading apps, including Libby and the Kindle app, give access to the world of books.

For this reason, I included an iPad in my testing. The iPad Mini made my list because it is the perfect size to feel like you're reading a paperback novel versus larger iPad models like the 9th generation, which feel like reading a clunky magazine.

Sources indicate that buying an e-reader is a far more significant investment than going to the bookstore. Plus, you still have to buy e-books. At first glance, it seems like an expensive adventure. Luckily, even with an e-reader, you can support your local library. With Libby, you can borrow and read audio and e-books from your local library and get them on your digital e-reader.

Industry observers note that libby has an iOS app and can instantly send books to your Kindle. If you don't happen to have a Kindle or iPad, you can still upload your library books through Adobe Digital Edition. Aka, you can still support your local library — and not pay a single penny to read a newly introduced book.

Considering the current state of affairs, the best gifts for the women in our lives are the ones that let them mentally clock out for a bit. The world is on fire—literally and figuratively. Plastic is melting onto corals, the measles are back, and just to kick us while we’re down, the girlies can’t even enjoy a Caesar salad or some chips and guac in peace. Some days, I'll catch myself staring at the sky and think, I wish I could hitch a ride to space, but of course, Elon Musk has ruined that fantasy for me, too.

Industry observers note that if the woman in your life is exhausted by the headlines, by the slow-motion collapse of democracy, by the sheer audacity of men in power, or perhaps just the overall state of humanity, she deserves a treat. Industry observers note that here are the best gifts for women surviving the dystopian quest that is 2026. For more thoughtful gift ideas for women, check out Gifts for Moms, Best Graduation Gifts, and Best Stocking Stuffers.

In a recent development, she’s been carrying the weight of the world for far too long. Therabody’s ThermBack LED melts away tension with targeted heat, vibration, LED, and far-infrared therapies. With three heat levels (up to 113 degrees Fahrenheit) and three vibration patterns (low, high, and wave), it stimulates circulation, loosens tight muscles in the lower back, and offers relief when she’s sitting at her desk for eight hours trying not to scream. It also doubles as a soothing heat pad for period cramps. Best of all, it automatically shuts off, so she doesn’t have to worry about turning it off. Check out some other options in our guide to the Best Massagers.

Recent findings suggest that when in doubt, perfume makes a lovely gift. A beautifully bottled eau de parfum inherently feels luxurious, but fragrance is a personal territory, so it’s best to avoid anything too polarizing unless you know her tastes. One safe and elegant bet: Bulgari’s Omnia Amethyste Eau de Parfum. Its soft, floral-woody scent is pleasant to wear year-round on its own or layer with her existing favorites. The composition opens with iris petal and ambrette accords, blooms into iris absolute and Damask rose, then settles into a warm, earthy base of bourbon vanilla and cistus labdanum absolute.

Industry observers note that women are expected to do it all, so why shouldn’t their alarm clocks? The Hatch Sleep Clock is a multitasking marvel. Along with being one of the best sunrise clocks on the market, it’s also a dimmable bedside light, a sound machine, and the first Hatch device to offer contactless sleep tracking. That last bit means she can monitor her slumber without strapping yet another gadget to her body. To unlock Hatch’s full audio library, she’ll need a Hatch+ membership ($6 per month), so I'd spring for at least three months. Consider it an investment in everyone’s well-being when she’s finally getting her beauty sleep.

Industry observers note that I absolutely adore Quince’s Mongolian cashmere collection. The Oversized Boyfriend Cardigan is the ultimate wardrobe staple for three out of four seasons. It’s not just perfect for sweata-weatha fall; it’s also cozy for rainy spring days and during the chill of winter. The fisherman rib detailing is uber-coastal, a charming touch to an already flattering and versatile piece. If your giftee is more of a sweatshirt gal, you also can't go wrong with the Fisherman Pullover Hoodie ($120) or the Full-Zip Hoodie ($120).

Everyone and their mother has an LED mask these days. If the woman in your life doesn’t, congratulations: You’ve found her gift. Chances are the Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask is already on her wishlist. And if it isn't, she simply hasn’t done enough research. The CryoGlow delivers red, infrared, and blue light, which is everything your face could possibly need short of a dermatologist. Its preset routines live on an attached controller, so there’s no troubleshooting. The real selling point, though, is the under-eye cooling pads, which help reduce puffiness and add a therapeutic element to the experience. I gifted one to my mother, and now she has to actively defend it from her friends.

In a recent development, get her the Eva Wearable Vibrator. A hands-free clitoral stimulation toy that can be used solo, but is best during penetrative sex. It’s tiny. It’s mighty. It’s hands-free (!!!), made of soft silicone, with three intensity levels. Gift the Eva to your best friend, or to your partner if you want to spice things up, in which case, you’re welcome.

If I have to feed myself, I want a kitchen appliance that does most of my labor. The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Noir is that appliance. She’s goth. She’s gorgeous. She air-fries, slow-cooks, and bakes with zero complaints. There are 11 preset functions, to be exact. I don’t know what all of them do, and I don’t care, because she knows. I don’t want to think about settings, and with Breville’s Element iQ system, which auto-adjusts temperature for precision cooking, I don’t have to. There’s even an app, which I didn’t download because I’m busy. You can check out more of our Air Fryer picks here.

Sources indicate that if she already owns an LED mask, it’s time to give her scalp the same VIP treatment. Red-light therapy isn’t just for pattern baldness; it may also help women experiencing all types of hair thinning and shedding, including postpartum hair loss. It can also help calm the scalp, increase blood flow, and regulate oil production. Reviewer Nena Farrell loves the HigherDose Red Light Hat, which is relatively affordable compared with competitors and looks like an ordinary baseball cap. That means she can take her self-care outside, and no one would ever know. How would they know?

Industry observers note that if she’s training for a marathon, tracking her stress cycles, or just wants hard data to justify why she feels like garbage, the Oura Ring 5 is the most stylish health tracker out there. Packed with advanced sensors, it monitors heart rate, skin temperature, sleep quality, and stress levels. It's also one of the only wearables that can reliably predict my menstrual cycle. Plus, it works with both Android and iOS, so she’s not locked into a single tech ecosystem.

The BrüMate Togosa gets it. It’s a wine chiller, pitcher, or whatever you need it to be because we no longer have the patience for single-purpose objects. Slide in a prechilled bottle, twist the lid shut, and let the BevGuard triple insulation keep your drink icy without ice, condensation, or a watery demise. When the vibe shifts from pinot to sangria, swap out the chiller lid and pour in your batch of whatever (up to 49 ounces). The leakproof strainer lid also keeps fruit, ice, and other garnishes from pouring through. And because being checked out of Earth doesn’t mean trashing it, its lids are made from 13 recycled water bottles, some finishes are dishwasher-safe to conserve water usage, and the vessel itself is built to last a lifetime. (If for some reason it doesn’t, BrüMate also offers a lifetime warranty.).

She may not be able to move to another planet, but she can build a 3D model of the Milky Way from the comfort of her home. This 3,000-ish piece LEGO set recreates the spiral galaxy, turning our jumbled universe into galactic home decor. The finished piece can be mounted on the wall as a daily reminder that Earth is just one of billions of planets we believe exist—surely, at least one of them has better men.

The Everywhere Tote is for the woman who is going where the universe takes her. It has everything one might need for far-flung travels: a 16-inch padded laptop sleeve, a handful of interior pockets, and a water-resistant nylon exterior for when you’re caught in an otherworldly atmospheric anomaly. Available in elemental shades like coast blue, sea green, and clay pink—it’s at home anywhere, from the gym to an impromptu odyssey. If she needs to jet off on a moment’s notice, it’s got a key clip, a trolley sleeve, and an exterior pocket for her wallet and passport. It also meets airlines’ personal item requirements.

Sources indicate that sometimes, the only way to check out is to beam yourself into another world, preferably one with juicier plotlines. This projector has 450 ISO lumens and 1080p resolution, with 4K support and color calibration. The gimbal stand tilts 165 degrees for projecting on walls, ceilings, or the back of an RV. The included hard-shell case is great for portability and easy storage. It runs for 2.5 hours on a single charge, and it's power bank-compatible, so you can watch from anywhere. Its AI-powered setup takes care of autofocus, screen fit, obstacle avoidance, and keystone correction, so she doesn't have to fiddle with settings with every tectonic shake. For more projectors, check out our guide.

Cozy Earth’s Bamboo Pajama Set is one of my favorite sets to wear on a lazy Sunday. The button-up pocketed design features chic contrast piping that lends a hotel-style aesthetic. They make me want to put on my LED mask, pick up my Kindle, and sip on sleepy girl mocktails until I doze off. Made from 95 percent bamboo viscose and 5 percent spandex, this knit blend is cooler and more breathable than cotton. Cozy Earth introduces fresh colors and prints each season, though the lighter shades can be somewhat sheer. If your giftee is over 5 foot 7 inches, I recommend the tall inseam. Sizes range from XXS to XXXL.

These Speks Odds Silicone Fidget Magnets are here to help you survive your stay in the stress-stricken simulation. Each set comes with three palm-sized magnets, encased in soft, textured silicone, designed to keep your hands busy while your brain zones out. I can’t stop fiddling with them when I’m watching TV and during Zoom calls. I can’t risk losing them by taking them outside, so they’ve found a home on my desk.

Speks also sells starter kits and gift bundles packed with other fidget toys. I loved the Moon Jelly Gump Memory Gel Stress Ball, until I handed it to my boyfriend for five minutes and he popped it. Men ruin everything.

Sources indicate that walking home alone at night on this planet is an absolute nightmare. If she can’t teleport away from creeps, she can at least blast a 130-decibel siren and flashing strobe light in their direction. The Birdie is a small but mighty alarm that will (hopefully) deter attackers and alert anyone nearby for help.

Industry observers note that I’ve used the original model for over a year (see my thoughts in my guide to the Best Personal Safety Alarms), and it’s given me peace of mind whenever I’m walking solo. The Birdie+, which I have yet to test, adds some useful features like location sharing, emergency support, and even a fake call function for a quick exit strategy. Plus, it comes in the cutest patterns. My one caveat is that this wouldn't be my first choice for a birthday gift or Valentine's Day, as it's kind of a downer.

In a recent development, she’s carrying her team at work, her family, and the knowledge that a recession is potentially looming. Don’t make her carry her water bottle, too. WanderFull’s Hydrobags have a thick, comfortable strap that takes a little bit of the load off her shoulders and come in dozens of colors and materials (including a newly introduced clear stadium line), one of which is sure to match her vibe. All Hydrobags bags can hold any handle-less water bottle up to 11 inches tall and 3.5 inches in diameter and sport two pockets for her phone and cards. If you can’t redistribute the household labor, the least you could do is redistribute the weight of her emotional-support beverage. —Kat Merck.

#1902. Tech Report: Best Laptops for Travel (2026): Which to Take on the Road
