Why Sony's latest digital Walkmans cost thousands of dollars

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The numbers on Sony’s latest Walkmans raise some questions that the spec sheets don’t answer.
  • Some of us have never owned a Walkman, and judging by the sticker prices of the latest models, that may never change.
  • The implied explanation for those insane prices is the premium components and materials Sony uses across the models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The numbers on Sony’s latest Walkmans raise some questions that the spec sheets don’t answer.

Some of us have never owned a Walkman, and judging by the sticker prices of the latest models, that may never change. Sony never stopped making them, though, and on October 15 the company opened pre-orders for three latest models. The cheapest, the NW-ZX900, costs a staggering $1,899. The NW-WM1AM3 sits above it at $2,999, while the gold-plated NW-WM1ZM3 flagship will set you back almost six grand.

The implied explanation for those insane prices is the premium components and materials Sony uses across the models. And while those parts aren't cheap, they don't explain why both less-expensive models cost more than twice what their predecessors did. They also don't explain why the $5,899 flagship offers no significant improvement on paper over the NW-ZX900, with essentially the same output from the headphone amp and a shorter battery life, at up to 33 hours of hi-res playback. Nor do they explain why that flagship works out to about $3,800 in Japan once sales tax is taken out. It's clear Sony is selling these as luxury goods to a small audiophile market, but as with a lot of audiophile gear, the returns shrink fast as the price goes up.

In a recent development, the $5,899 WM1ZM3 flagship's main chassis is machined from 99.99 percent pure oxygen-free copper and then gold-plated. The previous flagship's aluminum rear panel gets swapped for a copper one, and even the screws get a low-resistance gold plating, which Sony claims gives a more stable ground connection and, in turn, stronger bass and a wider soundstage. Inside, there's thick Kimber Kable wiring borrowed from Sony's DMP-Z1 desktop player, a second large polymer capacitor and a copper block over the digital circuitry that's 34 percent heavier than before. All that metal weighs a hefty 670g (around 1.5 pounds), up from the 2022 model's 490g (around 1.1 pounds).

The more modest $1,899 ZX900, meanwhile, has a machined aluminum chassis with a gold-plated copper rear panel, just like the $2,999 WM1AM3, and the same ultra-low-noise voltage regulator and crystal oscillators as its pricier siblings. All three use Sony's S-Master HX digital amp and are rated at 250mW per channel from the 4.4mm balanced jack, while storage goes from 64GB to 128GB to 256GB. So for the extra $4,000 between the ZX900 and the flagship, you're getting copper, better wiring, capacitors and more storage.

In its review of the $3,699 WM1ZM2, What Hi-Fi? pointed out that the (much) cheaper WM1AM2 shared most of the flagship's specs and engineering, and docked the ZM2 points for its limited power output. That's not addressed by the ZM3, either, since it's rated for the same 250mW per channel. AV Watch heard more of a step-up in transparency and space from the ZM2, but still called the AM2 excellent value for money. If an extra $2,300 paid for a difference that reviews couldn't agree on back in 2022, it's difficult to see how one could justify the $4,000 gap between the ZX900 and the ZM3 today.

Sources indicate that the NW-WM1Z, Sony's gold-plated Walkman from 2016, debuted at $3,199. In 2022, the WM1ZM2 became Sony's $3,699 Walkman for over-the-top audiophiles alongside a $1,399 WM1AM2. The ZX707 followed in 2023 at $899. This year, the WM1ZM3's price has jumped 59 percent, but both cheaper models have also more than doubled in price, meaning there's no longer a premium Walkman option under $1,000. Astell&Kern's Android-based SP4000 flagship, meanwhile, lists at $4,290, or about $1,600 less than the ZM3.

Retailers in Japan expect the WM1ZM3 to sell for around ¥655,000 and the ZX900 for around ¥215,000. Take out the 10 percent consumption tax that's included in Japanese shelf prices and convert at September's average of about ¥156 to the dollar, and that's roughly $3,800 and $1,250. In other words, US buyers are paying more than 50 percent more for the same players. Copper hit a record of around $14,850 a metric ton in August, but even a 670g (around 1.5 pounds) Walkman made entirely of copper would only contain about $10 worth of it.

Sources indicate that so if you're not already someone who will happily spend thousands on headphones and amps, the Walkman for you is still the NW-A306, which debuted at $349 in 2023 and is still on sale. The fresh trio replaces Sony's high-end players, not that one, and if you're set on one of them, the ZX900 gets you most of the flagship's hardware for the money. In essence, Sony has built all three Walkmans from expensive parts. But the jump in price since the previous generation looks like it has more to do with what die-hard audiophiles will pay for one, rather than what they cost to build.

#1879. “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2572 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

“Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs.
  • These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years.
  • These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he mentioned in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

Sources indicate that what got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.

It has been revealed that this group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.

How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?

Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.

According to recent reports, yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.

In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously demonstrated that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation—though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters that correlate with how we typically categorize races.

According to recent reports, skin tone and color do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin color, for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa, and Asia, rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim.

We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supported today. Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics.

In a recent development, recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.

In a recent development, while human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favor of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.

When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.

Sources indicate that hereditarians have relied heavily on a database that claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed. It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.

The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigor. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the Flynn effect, showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.

What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic—something that is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.

Industry observers note that as one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper, race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis—the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social challenges. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating, and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating—the complexities of our rich social lives.

In a recent development, not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning. These all involve our social relationships, and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.

Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioral sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioral diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning—not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.

In a recent development, rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory,” for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. In doing so, they make unsupportable assumptions about environmental differences between Africa and the rest of the world. They also fail to acknowledge half a century of research on the evolution of human cognitive ability.

Yes, we needed to learn new food gathering practices and methods for dealing with environmental challenges as we migrated across the world. But the same was true as humans migrated across the large and ecologically diverse continent of Africa. Race scientists provide no evidence for their arguments. They don’t rely on archaeological evidence, nor do they use typical methods from evolutionary biology to understand evolutionary processes. Using the methods of race scientists, it would be equally easy to make the argument that challenges posed by hot summers drove the evolution of higher intelligence, and equally without scientific backing.

No matter which way you look at these concerns—from the view of genetics, anthropology, evolutionary biology, or psychology—hereditarianism does not hold up.

To understand the potential consequences of these views, it is notable to see them in historical context. Early in the 20th century, race science was mainstream. Overly simplistic and biologically deterministic views about the origins of differences between human groups—not just race but class—were widespread (if not universal) and important to the eugenics movement.

If disadvantaged groups owe their disadvantage to some fault within them, and not to the structural conditions they experience, then some argue society is not responsible for helping those people. Such arguments led to eugenic sterilization laws that aimed to “improve” society by preventing—without their consent—the reproduction of those considered likely to pass on their innate “defects” to future children. And it was ultimately behind the Nazis’ “solution” of trying to eliminate “undesirables” entirely.

Industry observers note that in the decades after the Second World War, the horrors of the Nazi regime led to a decline in the popularity of eugenics in mainstream research and a rejection of race science. But the belief that science supported eugenic claims was already collapsing, even as the Nazis were trying to implement a race-based society. As we learned more about human biology and genetics during the 20th century, it became obvious that human genetic variation was too complex to be mapped into socially recognized racial (or class) categories. Advances in science meant race science dropped out of mainstream thinking.

Industry observers note that yet those committed to a belief in a biological hierarchy of races, regardless of what the science mentioned, wanted venues in which they could continue their discussions. In the 1960s, the pseudo-scientific journal Mankind Quarterly became their venue. Mankind Quarterly was funded by the Pioneer Fund, a nonprofit foundation set up in the 1930s by a US textile magnate who chose to use his fortune to fund research on race science and fight desegregation in the US.

Recent findings suggest that the Pioneer Fund continued to fund race science into the 21st century—including supporting Mankind Quarterly—when it was taken over by the current network of race scientists. They channeled its remaining funds into a upcoming firm, the Human Diversity Foundation, subsequently rebranded as Polygenic Scores LLC.

Sources indicate that given all this, how is race science still being published in mainstream academic journals? To be clear, race science does not typically get published in genetics or evolutionary biology journals. Most academic journals operate peer review, meaning papers only get published after evaluation by experts in the field. The overall absence of race science in genetics or biology journals is a clear signal that it does not meet contemporary standards of scientific rigor in genetics or biology.

According to recent reports, instead, race scientists continue to publish in para-scientific journals. But race science also makes it into a growing number of mainstream social science or humanities journals. Psychologist Andrew Winston, an expert in the history of race science in psychology, has described it as a “community project… with its own networks, mentorships, journals, funding, conferences, heroes, origin myths, martyrs, defenders, and historiography.”.

In a recent development, behind the network of writers producing race science sits a community of editors, peer reviewers, and others in gatekeeping roles, which too often allows race science to be published in mainstream journals. This is particularly in the subfields of psychology interested in intelligence and individual differences, and evolutionary psychology.

Editors of Intelligence, the mainstream journal that has probably published the largest quantity of race science, have occasionally published editorials defending their publication of race science in the name of ensuring robust academic debate even on controversial topics.

There have been sanctions. Philippe Rushton, one of an earlier generation of race scientists, faced sanctions from his university in Canada but kept his job apparently owing to the intervention of Edward O. Wilson, arguably the most famous biologist toward the end of the 20th century.

Cofnas created justified controversy over his call for a “hereditarian revolution” after which it will be acknowledged that black people are innately intellectually disadvantaged compared to white people. But he kept his postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge University (though his affiliation with a Cambridge college was ended). He has also kept his postdoctoral position at Ghent University after using the opportunity provided by excessive news coverage of Arday to publicize his hereditarian views (though some sanctions have been imposed, such as restrictions on teaching). Cofnas has defended his views by saying he’s been misunderstood and is entitled to free inquiry.

Moreover, when University College London discovered that the race science community had been holding conferences on its premises (the “London Conferences on Intelligence”), without their knowledge of the subject of the conferences, they acted to prevent further such conferences being held. The publisher of the journal Intelligence, Elsevier, has recently appointed upcoming editors, who have stated their commitment to publishing both rigorous and socially responsible science. Race scientists are increasingly publishing in evolutionary psychology journals rather than Intelligence.

It has been revealed that however, the London Conferences on Intelligence continue, though not at UCL. Race scientists also have a media arm, Aporia magazine, which promotes race science using much more overt language and with more obvious policy focus than publications in academic journals. One Aporia article, for example, argued for eugenics as a solution to Africa’s lack of economic development, noting in a post that some may find it “distasteful.” It claimed—relying on race science’s unscientific arguments—that artificial selection for higher intelligence is needed to improve the continent’s innately unintelligent populace.

Race science may not have the respect of the scientific community, but it does have funding and influential backers. A report by Hope not Hate revealed that the network of race scientists received significant funding from the US businessman Andrew Conru, who withdrew his funding after the report was released.

The US Ambassador to Belgium even intervened when Ghent University set up an investigation into how Cofnas was hired.

Race scientists are far from the victims they claim to be. Race scientists in this and previous generations have worked hard to ensure their messages are heard beyond academia. And in this generation, they are successfully using social media to spread their beliefs, especially Elon Musk’s X.

But what about academic freedom? Isn’t it good for science to discuss any hypothesis to ensure free exchange of ideas? Academic debate is productive only if it involves methodologically rigorous research. Science will not progress if one side of any debate consistently uses poor-quality, methodologically flawed work. Nor is it necessary to continually debate topics that have long since been settled.

We believe it is unequivocal that race science is fundamentally pseudoscience. In our view, it’s critical to call attention to not only the scientific flaws underlying this body of work but also the real target it’s aimed at: political actors and everyday readers who ultimately decide the direction that science, and society, goes in.

In a recent development, jonathan R. Goodman is Assistant Research Professor, Psychiatry, University of Cambridge, and Rebecca Sear is Director of the Centre for Culture and Evolution, Brunel University of London.

The Outages Are Just Getting Started

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
  • In a recent development, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
  • Recent findings suggest that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

In a recent development, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

Recent findings suggest that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials mentioned this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

External pressures and bugs in patches are not upcoming, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

Recent findings suggest that “Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” states Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

According to recent reports, “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” states Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

According to recent reports, matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These fresh threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

According to recent reports, in the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are key nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik notes. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

According to recent reports, only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

It has been revealed that “What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” claims Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

According to recent reports, • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech organization was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

Anthropic’s record IPO collides with tech’s worst week on Wall Street since 2020

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his home in Silicon Valley.
  • "This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the firm.
  • It has been revealed that anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Startup investor Ben Narasin is so jazzed about Anthropic's blockbuster IPO that he's planning a party later this month at his home in Silicon Valley. Sake, vodka and Krug Champagne will be served. Each attendee will be given two jars of caviar.

"This is a celebration of the most material, significant, and mind-blowingly awesome event that has ever happened in venture capital," Narasin, founding partner of Tenacity Venture Capital, told CNBC in an interview, adding that he didn't even invest in the firm.

It has been revealed that anthropic raised a record $93.5 billion in its IPO and an additional $26 billion from tech giants that bought at the offer price. The stock gained 17% in its debut on Thursday, lifting Anthropic's market cap to $1.8 trillion and providing a much-needed windfall for Silicon Valley's startup ecosystem.

It has been revealed that it was quite the split-screen moment on Wall Street, which spent the week in an AI-driven tailspin. Led by Nvidia's 23% plunge, which marked the stock's sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, the Nasdaq slid 10% over the past five trading days in its worst week since the early days of Covid in 2020.

Investors and analysts spent the week debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware, as it's reliant on advanced chips, memory and data centers, or whether it will stand alone as the first public pure-play AI developer and a organization that's achieved unrivaled growth in less than six years of existence.

Sources indicate that that question will likely persist for some time, but Friday's market action showed that Wall Street is skeptical of Anthropic's ability to grow into its lofty valuation. At week's end, the Claude creator's $1.6 trillion fully diluted market cap put it behind just six U.S. companies: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Amazon and SpaceX.

With the tech market in turmoil due to rising interest rates, raging anti-AI sentiment and Nvidia's C-suite crisis, Anthropic's IPO was part exuberance, part relief for an industry hungry for exits.

After venture-backed IPOs yielded $73 billion in proceeds in 2021, the amount raised in the next four years totaled just $39 billion, according to data from University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter. In 2021, 126 technology companies went public, compared with 34 in 2025.

Meanwhile, the private market has continued to balloon, with companies raising ever-larger sums at sky-high valuations without the pressures of quarterly earnings. Many startups that had hoped to go public early in the decade fell out of favor in the AI boom. They experienced hefty job cuts, down rounds and acquisitions for pennies on the dollar.

"There was a time in Silicon Valley not that long ago where the prevailing wisdom was the default path should be avoiding going public for as long as possible," mentioned Somesh Dash, a general partner at venture firm IVP. The view was, "it's too long, it's too hard, it's not worth it," he said.

Sources indicate that anthropic is very young compared to some of those companies, but it was a huge collector of private capital. Investors poured $141 billion into the AI lab as of September, according to Anthropic's prospectus.

Recent findings suggest that for a few Silicon Valley firms that contributed to those funding rounds, the returns are unlike anything they've ever seen. At the IPO price, Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners each owned about $25 billion worth of Anthropic stock. Bessemer Venture Partners owned a stake worth roughly $10 billion, partner Byron Deeter said.

Matt Murphy, a partner at Menlo, told CNBC's David Faber on Thursday that his firm has more than five limited partners "that we delivered over $1 billion of returns to.".

Recent findings suggest that "At the end of the day, that's really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments," Murphy stated. "There's a lot of pride in being able to do that.".

Bessemer's Deeter was also jubilant on Thursday, posting on X that, in addition to being "the largest bet in Bessemer's history," the IPO "is a punctuation mark in the history of both humanity and computation.".

According to recent reports, that's quite a change from a few years earlier, when Anthropic was hardly generating revenue, and success was far from guaranteed. In 2023, Anthropic's Claude 2 was struggling to keep pace with models from Google and OpenAI. In April 2024, investors at Bessemer wrote in a memo that if Anthropic were to miss its own targets, there was "a good chance that we lose all or part of our money.".

Guru Chahal at Lightspeed told CNBC that Anthropic was clearly the team taking a more measured approach to AI. The organization looked beyond Nvidia's dominant AI chips, choosing to also use alternatives from Amazon and Google. Anthropic said it generated $1.72 in revenue per dollar spent on computing power in the third quarter, up from 68 cents a year earlier.

"It is true that it required lots of capital, but when you dig in and you realize that capital is going toward compute, and this is the team that's positioned to use that compute in the most effective way, then we could connect those dots," Chahal said. He added that those metrics highlighted it was "going to be a very high-quality business.".

Anthropic isn't the only significant win for VCs this year.

Five months before Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, SpaceX hit the market in what, until this week, was by far the largest IPO in history. SpaceX, which Elon Musk founded in 2002, produced outsized returns for firms including Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz.

SpaceX and Anthropic alone will turn 2026 into a monster year for the venture industry, easily exceeding any other in terms of IPO proceeds. And investors in OpenAI hope appetite remains strong for trillion-dollar companies next year, as the ChatGPT maker is looking to 2027 for a potential offering.

IVP's Dash noted that in his AI portfolio, "a lot of companies are starting IPO prep" even if it's only "year four, year five, year six since inception." He hopes to see at least half a dozen companies go public at valuations north of $10 billion each in the second half of 2027.

The macro picture, however, is ominous.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia has left the chip giant without a clear leader at a time when the manufacturer already faced heightened concerns about a slowdown in spending. Nvidia is a key investor in Anthropic and OpenAI and a critical supplier and financing partner for the entire AI industry, which is getting hammered across the board.

In January, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate after this month's midterm elections, which included the passage of numerous ballot measures that could stymie data center development. Anthropic investor Brad Gerstner predicted after the election that market dynamics would lead Anthropic to price toward the lower end of its range.

Narasin stated he wasn't even sure the company would get that far.

"I was concerned they'd delay," Narasin noted.

That makes the outcome that much more impressive, he said, after Anthropic priced above its expected range and upsized the offering.

Recent findings suggest that "This will be bedtime stories for years for future VCs," Narasin mentioned. "There was a manufacturer that was created, backed by angels and later venture" that in a few short years "became the single biggest IPO of all history.".

— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

#1874. What are the actual differences between cheap and expensive sound systems?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1554 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

What are the actual differences between cheap and expensive sound systems?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spending more doesn't guarantee a better fit for you, though there are some clear differences as you climb in price.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Your TV's built-in speakers are fine...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spending more doesn't guarantee a better fit for you, though there are some clear differences as you climb in price.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Your TV's built-in speakers are fine... if you don't care about hearing dialogue clearly, feeling the bass or knowing where an explosion is coming from. Even an inexpensive soundbar can make a noticeable difference.

Soundbars can range from around $100 to well over $1,000, as demonstrated by our picks for the best soundbars. Many highly rated models that provide good value fall between $200 and $600 in our findings, as well as those from other outlets like Consumer Reports. The options vary considerably in how they handle surround sound, from basic bars designed to improve dialogue to more elaborate systems with wireless subwoofers and rear speakers.

Diminishing returns are key here. The biggest improvements usually come from moving beyond TV speakers and entry-level soundbars. After that, you're paying for more capable hardware, additional features and refinements that may be less noticeable to the average listener. Let's look at a couple of different price buckets, which aren't exact quality dividers but will give you an idea.

A basic soundbar can make dialogue easier to hear and give movies more presence. Models under $100 are pretty stripped-down and have limited connectivity, fewer sound modes and can't reproduce deep bass. They're designed to improve everyday TV audio without needing a complicated setup.

At this price, you're typically looking at a 2.0 or 2.1 setup. If you're not familiar with speaker channel numbers, a 2.0 soundbar has two audio channels (stereo), while a 2.1 model adds a separate subwoofer to handle lower frequencies. The Hisense HS2100, for example, sells for around $120 and includes a wireless subwoofer that gives it a fuller sound than a standalone bar.

Sources indicate that for just under $200, you can get considerably more hardware. The Hisense HS5100 is a 5.1-channel system (adding two rear speakers and a center channel compared to 2.1) with a dedicated subwoofer and satellite speakers. Instead of relying on processing to simulate surround sound, the rear speakers provide audio behind you. It doesn't support Dolby Atmos, though, so you don't get overhead effects.

This is where soundbars start offering more impressive improvements to your TV's audio. You should see features like eARC for sending audio to your soundbar from any other input, as well as Wi-Fi streaming and more robust app features like full EQ management. You might also get upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos, making compatible movie soundtracks more immersive. Exact features vary among models; for example, the Hisense AX3120Q is a 3.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar for around $280.

Sources indicate that A 3.1.2 system has three front-facing channels, a subwoofer and two height channels. That gives you a dedicated center channel for dialogue and hardware designed to reproduce overhead effects. The Polk Signa S4 is another example for around $449, while Sony's Bravia Theater Bar 5 offers a less expensive $350 alternative with a dedicated subwoofer and 3.1-channel configuration, virtualizing the overhead and directional effects. Neither gives you separate rear speakers for physical surround sound.

At the upper end of this price range, there are more complete surround systems with dedicated rear speakers and multiple height channels. The Hisense AX5140Q is a 5.1.4-channel system with a wireless subwoofer, two satellite speakers and four upward-firing drivers. It also includes features like a graphic equalizer, independent channel adjustments and dialogue enhancement. That's a lot more hardware than you'll find in a basic soundbar.

In this range, you'll find more capable surround sound systems, but the improvements aren't just about adding more speakers. The Samsung HW-Q800F offers 5.1.2-channel audio with a wireless subwoofer and up-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos. It doesn't include rear speakers, though; it uses side-firing drivers for virtual surround effects. Other models, like Samsung's 3.1.2-channel HW-QS700F soundbar, offer features like automatic adjustments based on whether the bar is on a TV stand or a wall.

The JBL Bar 1000MK2 offers another step up. Its 7.1.4-channel configuration includes detachable, battery-powered satellite speakers, a subwoofer and upward-firing drivers. It also has room correction and a graphic equalizer. The detachable speakers give you physical surround sound when you want it, without having to keep them out permanently.

Recent findings suggest that at the upper end of this range, you have systems like Marshall's $1,000 Dolby Atmos Heston 120 soundbar. But spending more doesn't necessarily mean getting a better fit for your room.

A dedicated home theater system gives you more control over where sound comes from. Instead of using a soundbar to simulate surround effects, an AV receiver sends audio to individual speakers around your room. A basic 5.1 setup includes left and right front speakers, a center channel, two rear surround speakers and a subwoofer.

The difference isn't just about having more speakers, though. A properly configured surround system can create a more convincing sense of space and make it easier to hear where dialogue and sound effects are coming from. But the difference between surround sound systems and soundbars shows with tradeoffs in cost, space and setup complexity.

If you're willing to invest in separate components, a receiver-based system gives you more room to customize and upgrade later. Home Audio Advice put together a roughly $1,300 setup using a Yamaha RX-V4A receiver and a Klipsch Reference Cinema 5.1.4 speaker package. The receiver powers a basic 5.1 setup and the Klipsch package includes four additional height-effect speakers that can be used after upgrading to a compatible receiver. The flexibility is a major advantage.

However, soundbars are still able to offer a convincing surround experience. Samsung's 11.1.4-channel HW-Q990D soundbar is an example, though it doesn't come cheap. There are also modular options like LG's Dolby Atmos FlexConnect home theater system, which let you arrange compatible speakers around your room without committing to traditional wired placement.

In a recent development, one of the biggest differences between inexpensive and premium speakers is how accurately they portray the sound captured by media creators. A speaker with an uneven response may emphasize certain frequencies while making others harder to hear, while a more balanced frequency response produces a more natural sound.

Bass reproduction is another area where better equipment makes a noticeable difference. Low-frequency extension describes how deep a bass signal a speaker can play before it starts dropping off. Smaller speakers struggle with the lowest frequencies, which is why a subwoofer makes such a difference in a home theater.

Industry observers note that louder isn't necessarily better, but a system able to maintain sound quality at higher volume definitely matters. More capable speakers can deliver greater output while maintaining a more consistent sound, which is helpful in larger rooms or when listening at high volumes.

The jump from TV speakers to an inexpensive soundbar is usually a lot more noticeable than moving from a midrange to a premium one. Even soundbars under $300 can give a substantial improvement, and some budget models deliver sound quality that competes with more expensive options. Consumer Reports has found that certain less expensive soundbars rival pricier models in overall sound quality. Spending more isn't pointless, but the improvements become less direct as you move up the price ladder.

Industry observers note that at higher price points, you're typically paying for refinements instead of a completely different audio experience. Those improvements can matter if you have a large space, watch a lot of movies, are a serious gamer or want to customize your setup over time. But someone watching content that doesn't take advantage of modern audio features (like news and sports) in a small living room may not notice enough of a difference to justify doubling their budget.

Recent findings suggest that your room can also limit the benefits of expensive equipment. Walls, floors, furniture and speaker placement all affect how sound travels, especially at lower frequencies. Before spending hundreds on upcoming equipment, try repositioning your speakers or changing where you sit; small changes to your audio setup can pay off.

If you're looking for clearer dialogue and better everyday TV audio, you probably don't need to spend more than $150 to $200. A basic 2.1 soundbar gives you fuller sound and deeper bass without taking up much space. Inexpensive soundbars will work particularly well in small and medium-sized rooms, which makes them a practical choice if you aren't looking for a full home theater experience.

If you watch a lot of movies or listen to music through your TV, spending around $250 to $500 gives you more options. This is where you can start finding dedicated center channels, Wi-Fi streaming and, depending on the model, physical rear speakers or Dolby Atmos.

Spending $500 to $1,000 or more makes sense if you want a more complete home theater experience, have a larger room or care about getting the most out of movies, games and music. At this level, you can find high-quality soundbars with multiple height channels, room correction and more customization options. You can also start building a component-based system, giving you more flexibility to upgrade over time.

Industry observers note that just remember that a higher price doesn't automatically mean a better fit. Consider your room, listening habits and the features you'll actually use before deciding how much to spend.

💡 Key Takeaways

Recent findings suggest that xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.

It has been revealed that after a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s fresh Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.

According to recent reports, the rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, massive batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.

According to recent reports, there are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Sources indicate that they come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.

In a recent development, the rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.

You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.

Sources indicate that unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.

The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.

It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.

According to recent reports, xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a latest third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.

It has been revealed that the ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.

Sources indicate that the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.

Sources indicate that the Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.

#1872. Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1646 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Sunrise on the Reaping review: The biggest and boldest Hunger Games yet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you?
  • Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell.
  • Recent findings suggest that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

Recent findings suggest that the question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

It has been revealed that this being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

It has been revealed that viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

After sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a latest variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

Industry observers note that then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

In a recent development, that vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

Drusilla is one of the fresh characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a massive chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace swiftly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating upcoming version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

According to recent reports, no spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

But while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.).

Throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up claims "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

It's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.).

According to recent reports, anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. In a recent development, in the immediate fallout of Jensen Huang’s humiliating resignation from Nvidia, coverage will focus on how the company looks to continue without its beloved former CEO, the world’s biggest champion of open-source AI and the proliferation of GPUs across borders. But in the long term, there’s an argument to be made that Google will be one of the largest winners of the shake-up, with a market opening up to competition outside of Nvidia’s CUDA moat.

While Colette Kress, the interim CEO, is unlikely to make any drastic changes to the manufacturer’s roadmap, the reality is that Nvidia’s competitors in the semiconductor space have desperately been working to unseat the market leader, and without Jensen at the helm, customers may be more likely to pursue alternatives.

For years, Google has offered its TPUs, or Tensor Processing Units, as a solution for AI training and inference, but they’ve been largely locked to its Google Cloud infrastructure. That’s changing now that the company is opening up sales to third parties and has revealed it will bring TPU capacity to Oracle’s cloud beginning in 2027.

Google’s latest generation of TPUs is specialized; here’s how the manufacturer describes the lineup in its recent announcement post:.

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning (inference), TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

In a recent development, google isn’t comparing its fresh TPUs directly to Nvidia’s offerings, and clock-for-clock, even the most powerful TPU 8i Max doesn’t touch Vera Rubin for sheer performance. But this generation should be much more competitive for a few reasons: it’s more power efficient in certain configurations, and Google made it easier to translate coding workflows optimized for CUDA to work with its TPUs.

Back in October, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, which it co-developed with Meta’s PyTorch team, to let developers use familiar PyTorch workflows on TPUs with minimal code changes. That won’t make every custom CUDA operation portable or eliminate performance tuning, but reducing the effort required to try an alternative may change the buying decision. Customers don’t need to abandon Nvidia outright for Google to increase its TPU market share, or for Nvidia to face more pressure on price.

In a recent development, alongside Broadcom and MediaTek, Google is taking on the Nvidia behemoth, and in the short term, it will almost certainly see a large upside in sentiment. But in the longer term, with scaling pressure lowering margins for Nvidia, Google’s specialized and more efficient TPUs may be a primary beneficiary of this sea change. They could also offset a slowdown in Search as Google’s shift to Cloud continues apace.

Sources indicate that the FAA describes a flood of connection attempts that destabilized its telecommunications network, affecting aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in Arkansas and Texas that were undergoing router and wire replacements, but even days after the stop was lifted, there’s still no clear underlying cause.

Meanwhile, the Microsoft 365 outage lasted about 30 hours, with service restored to the remaining customers and regions late Friday. Microsoft says that a “latent defect” introduced into its network code in a July revision wasn’t triggered until a few days ago, when high loads led to cascading failures across the firm’s servers worldwide.

While neither AI nor cyberattacks were to blame, individually and together the two outages add urgency to getting companies to shore up their defenses and redundancies in a world where we’re overly reliant on digital systems.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google is rolling out a major change to Gemini’s privacy settings, giving owners more control over how their conversations are stored and whether Google can use them to train its AI models.
  • Confirmed Monday, the change separates chat history from your AI training preferences, so you can still have your conversations saved without the contents being automatically used to improve Google’s models.
  • Recent findings suggest that until now, Gemini's Keep Activity setting did both jobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is rolling out a major change to Gemini’s privacy settings, giving owners more control over how their conversations are stored and whether Google can use them to train its AI models.

Confirmed Monday, the change separates chat history from your AI training preferences, so you can still have your conversations saved without the contents being automatically used to improve Google’s models.

Recent findings suggest that until now, Gemini's Keep Activity setting did both jobs. It determined how long conversations would be on offer and whether their contents could be used to improve Google’s generative AI models. That all-in-one approach is being split into two different controls.

First up is History, which allows owners to choose how long Gemini keeps their chats. The second independently controls whether chat content (text and attachments) can be used to train generative AI. For anyone who does want their previous conversations available but doesn't want to contribute them to Google's AI development efforts, it's a welcome change.

It has been revealed that there’s one privacy detail that is worth understanding. Disabling the new History option won’t immediately delete all conversations, nor will it prevent Google from temporarily storing new ones.

Industry observers note that future chats will still be saved for about two months, Google mentioned. Gemini uses this data to respond to consumers, process feedback, and support safety and security efforts, the company said. Humans may also look over these conversations for these purposes.

That is a huge change from past retention periods, which reportedly kept chat context available for 24 hours and safety-related data for 72 hours.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced controls will be rolled out globally to the Gemini app over the next few weeks. Users who have Keep Activity already disabled will have both new settings off by default. Google is emailing users about the changes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story.

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.”.

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly.

In a recent development, other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”.

In a recent development, there are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

This would make my decision to buy device like Clicks Communicator much easier.

In a recent development, as per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting.

In a recent development, iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

Recent findings suggest that on Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?
